design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of proportions (PROSPERO CRD42018086734; PRISMA and MOOSE) of cohort studies reporting how many people with a substance-induced, brief, atypical, not-otherwise-specified (NOS) or schizophreniform psychosis later received a diagnosis of schizophrenia (schizoaffective disorder combined with it), after at least 6 months of follow-up. MEDLINE, PsycINFO and Embase were searched for English-language peer-reviewed publications from 1980 to 2018, with hand-searching of reference lists. 50 studies gave 79 estimates in 40,783 people; 25 studies of substance-induced psychosis gave 43 substance-specific estimates, pooled by substance (5 estimates for amphetamines). Logit-transformed proportions in mixed-effects models (random effects within subgroups); categorical moderators by study-level subgroup analysis with a Bonferroni threshold of P < .01; continuous moderators by meta-regression; Egger's test for publication bias. Read: PMC full text PMC7147575 (all sections, Tables 1 to 5 rendered as text, funding, acknowledgements with the conflict-of-interest statement, author information and the reference list); Figure 1 (PRISMA flow chart) is an image and was not read for values; the supplementary material (a PDF with study-quality analyses and funnel plots) was not opened.
can_establish: The average proportion, across cohorts published to 2018, of people with a substance-induced psychosis who later received a diagnosis of schizophrenia, by substance, and how widely the studies differ, including a pooled 22% (14% to 34%) for amphetamine-induced psychoses.
cannot_establish: Whether amphetamine or methamphetamine use causes lasting schizophrenia or reveals an existing vulnerability (no comparison group; the authors use the term substance-induced by convention, not causally), what the risk is for a given person or follow-up period (I² 96% for amphetamines, follow-up of 1 to 20 years, follow-up completeness of 40% to 100% among the substance-induced cohorts), which studies make up the amphetamine pool (not named in the article), or whether that pool contains cocaine-induced psychoses (the methods group cocaine with methamphetamine and amphetamine as stimulants).

sample.recruitment: PsycINFO, MEDLINE and Embase via Ovid, 1980 to 2018, English-language peer-reviewed publications, with the full search string given; reference lists of identified studies hand-searched; 6097 records, 5906 excluded on abstract, 141 excluded on full text, 4 added by hand-searching, 50 studies (Methods › Search Strategy; Results › Search Results, 1st paragraph). The studies came from 25 countries; index diagnoses were made in hospital (27 studies) or in mixed hospital and community settings (13), by structured interview (22) or from routine clinical or register records (16) (Results › Search Results, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: a baseline diagnosis of substance-induced, brief, atypical, NOS or schizophreniform psychosis by DSM, ICD or other recognized criteria; a follow-up diagnosis in the same people at least 6 months later; and the number with schizophrenia at follow-up; case series, case-control and cohort studies and randomized trials. Excluded: psychosis defined by symptom scales or self-report; commentaries, book chapters, conference abstracts, editorials, reviews, single case studies, grey literature and qualitative studies; delusional disorder; for several reports on one cohort, all but the largest (Methods › Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria, 1st to 3rd paragraphs). Methamphetamine, amphetamine and cocaine psychoses were recorded as stimulant-induced, and MDMA, LSD, PCP and psilocybin psychoses as hallucinogen-induced (2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Mean study proportion male 61% (72% weighted by participants); mean study age 28 years (29 weighted); all but 8 studies were of first-episode cohorts; mean follow-up 4.0 years, stated range 1 to 20 years, 8.4 years weighted (Results › Search Results, 2nd paragraph). Almost no study reported demographics by diagnostic subgroup, so whole-study figures were used (Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph).
sample.attrition: Follow-up completeness is recorded per study (Table 1): among the 25 studies that include substance-induced psychosis it ranges from 40% (Kittirattanapaiboon 2010) to 100%, and across all 50 studies from 5% to 100% (editors' reading of Table 1). The percentage followed up was tested as a moderator (meta-regression β −1.716, P = .0785; Table 4).
sample.selection_effects: Mostly hospital-based cohorts identified at first admission or through registers, in which people with enduring disorders are more likely to stay in contact with services (a bias the authors raise for treatment cohorts, Introduction, 2nd paragraph), while people with brief episodes who are never admitted are missed; English-language peer-reviewed publications only, no grey literature; searches run by one author. Most participants in the substance-induced pool come from register studies dominated by alcohol-induced psychoses (19,358 of 34,224 in the alcohol subgroup). The review includes the corresponding author's own register study (Sara et al., 2014), for which the authors supplied additional data, and a cohort co-authored by J. Lappin (Heslin et al., 2015).

exposure.measurement: The exposure is the index diagnosis: substance-induced psychosis (by substance where reported) or brief, atypical, NOS or schizophreniform psychosis, by DSM, ICD or other criteria, from structured interview, routine clinical diagnosis or file review; toxicology was used in establishing the diagnosis in only 3 of the 25 studies of substance-induced psychosis (Table 3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not available: very few studies reported the amount or duration of substance use before the episode (Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Studies with mixed or unspecified substances form their own subgroup (19 estimates, 8447 people; Table 2). Comorbid substance use disorders at the index diagnosis and ongoing use during follow-up were rarely reported and could not be analysed, although the authors cite evidence that ongoing use is a critical risk factor for readmission and transition (Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; substance use during follow-up was not recorded in most studies.

comparison.controls: No unexposed comparison group: substance-induced psychoses are compared with brief, atypical and NOS psychoses (34 estimates, 5969 people) and schizophreniform psychosis (20 estimates, 590 people), and substances are compared with one another (Table 2).
comparison.matching: Not applicable. Comparisons between substances are mostly between studies; only three studies gave separate within-study estimates for cannabis and other substances (Discussion › Cannabis and Transition to Schizophrenia, 1st paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history, premorbid functioning, duration of untreated psychosis and symptom profiles were too rarely reported to be analysed (Discussion › Clinical and Service Implications, 4th paragraph; Limitations, 5th paragraph); a later Swedish study cited by the authors found familial risk scores twice as high in people whose substance-induced psychosis was followed by schizophrenia (Discussion › Cannabis and Transition to Schizophrenia, 2nd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Schizophrenia at follow-up (schizoaffective disorder added where reported separately), diagnosed by structured research interview (8 studies of substance-induced psychosis, 127 people), routine clinical diagnosis (10 studies, 15,059 people) or file review (7 studies, 19,038 people) (Table 3; Discussion › Limitations, 4th paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors note that routine diagnoses of substance-induced, brief and atypical psychoses are often imprecise (Discussion › Limitations, 4th paragraph). Study quality was rated with the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (median 5) (Results › Study Quality).
outcomes.operationalization: Proportion of the original cohort with a follow-up diagnosis of schizophrenia (Methods › Outcome and Moderator Variables, 1st paragraph); whether the denominator is everyone at baseline or only those followed up is not stated beyond this.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni threshold of P < .01 for the planned subgroup comparisons (11 categorical moderators in Table 3); no correction stated for the five meta-regressions (Table 4) or the comparison of seven substance subgroups (Methods › Meta-analysis, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two authors independently selected the studies and extracted all data, with a third resolving differences; the search was run by one author and reference lists were hand-searched by two (Methods › Search Strategy; Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria, 1st paragraph; Outcome and Moderator Variables, 2nd paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled proportions with 95% CIs (Table 2): substance-induced psychosis 25% (18 to 35), 25 estimates, 34,224 people, Q 3034, I² 99%; brief, atypical and NOS 36% (30 to 43), I² 92%; schizophreniform 65% (57 to 72), I² 54%; overall 44% (39 to 49). By substance: cannabis 34% (25 to 46), 6 estimates, 3040 people, I² 96%; hallucinogens 26% (14 to 43), 3 estimates, 208 people; amphetamines 22% (14 to 34), 5 estimates, 2284 people, Q 106, I² 96%; mixed or unspecified 22% (17 to 29), 19 estimates, 8447 people; opioids 12% (8 to 18), 3, 664; sedatives 10% (7 to 15), 2, 223; alcohol 9% (6 to 15), 5, 19,358, I² 97%; difference between substances Q 137, df 6, P < .0001. Categorical moderators (Table 3; Bonferroni threshold P < .01): none significant, for example national 20% (11 to 33) vs subnational 34% (28 to 40), P = .0559; urban 39% vs rural 19% vs mixed 22%, P = .0432; toxicology used 38% vs 24%, P = .1423; quality at or above the median 24% vs below 27%, P = .6683. Meta-regression (Table 4): average age β −0.050 (−0.095 to −0.005), P = .0286; percent male 2.298 (−0.492 to 5.087), P = .1065; length of follow-up −0.030 (−0.093 to 0.033), P = .3433; percent followed up −1.716 (−3.628 to 0.196), P = .0785; year of publication 0.004, P = .8892. No prediction intervals are reported.
analysis.covariates: None; moderators were examined one at a time.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42018086734 (Methods, 1st paragraph); the registered protocol was not compared with the review here. The planned meta-regressions on PANSS, BPRS and GAF scores, comorbid substance use and duration of psychosis could not be done for lack of data (Results › Subgroup Analysis; Discussion › Limitations, 5th paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Substance-specific estimates are not shown study by study in the article (no forest plot in the main text; the supplement was not opened), so the five amphetamine estimates and the studies they come from cannot be identified from the article.
analysis.power: Not addressed; several subgroups rest on two or three studies (sedatives 2, opioids 3, hallucinogens 3; rural 2, Europe 2, community 3), which the authors acknowledge makes subgroup estimates uncertain (Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 25 cohorts of substance-induced psychosis, the pooled proportion later diagnosed with schizophrenia was 25% (18% to 35%), with near-total heterogeneity (I² 99%); for amphetamines 22% (14% to 34%) from 5 estimates and 2284 people (I² 96%), for cannabis 34% and for alcohol 9%. No study feature predicted transition at the review's threshold for significance.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says that substance-induced psychoses associated with cannabis, hallucinogens and amphetamines "have a substantial risk of transition to schizophrenia" and that transition rates were not affected by sex, country, setting, diagnostic methods or duration of follow-up (Abstract). Gaps: (1) risk of transition here means later diagnoses in cohorts without any comparison group, which cannot show whether the substance caused a lasting illness, whether some index episodes were primary psychoses, or whether diagnostic rules relabelled persistent psychosis; the methods say the term substance-induced is used by convention and not as a causal claim (Methods, 1st paragraph), but the abstract does not; (2) not affected rests on non-significant tests across 25 heterogeneous studies with subgroups of two or three studies, and the percentage followed up came close (P = .0785), with more complete follow-up going with lower transition; (3) type of substance as the primary predictor is mostly a between-study comparison, with within-study support from three studies, all concerning cannabis; (4) the abstract gives the amphetamine figure without its heterogeneity (I² 96%). The discussion, in contrast, explains the ecological nature of the age association and lists the main limitations plainly.

timeline.event: Thai cohort of 1116 people with methamphetamine psychosis after a first hospitalisation (Kittirattanapaiboon et al.; reference 13), included here as 39% with schizophrenia after 5 years, with 40% of the cohort followed up (Table 1).
Finnish register study of 18,478 inpatients with substance-induced psychosis (Niemi-Pynttäri et al.; reference 16), included here as 6% for all substances together (Table 1).

Earlier meta-analysis of the diagnostic stability of first-episode psychosis (Fusar-Poli et al.; reference 18): 21% of 164 people in 10 studies with a substance-induced psychosis later diagnosed with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder (Introduction, 4th paragraph).
Commentary by two of this review's authors on methamphetamine-related psychosis as an opportunity for assertive intervention, cited in the clinical implications (reference 94)

Systematic review of methamphetamine-associated psychosis that reports the Thai cohort, with a second study, as 33–38% re-diagnosed after 6–7 years and a Finnish register figure of 16% within 16 years

Swedish national study published after this review's inclusion period (Kendler et al.; reference 99): cumulative hazard of schizophrenia 11.3% after any substance-induced psychosis and 18.0% after cannabis-induced psychosis (Discussion › Cannabis and Transition to Schizophrenia, 3rd paragraph).
Systematic review of antipsychotic treatment that cites this review's amphetamine figure with a misprinted interval
24-month randomized trial in stimulant-induced psychosis that cites this review and reports 7 of 137 participants (5.1%) newly diagnosed with schizophrenia within 24 months

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of transition to schizophrenia by substance identified here. Its amphetamine estimate (22%, 14% to 34%) gives a pooled figure where the encyclopedia had only single studies reported second-hand, but with I² 96%, component studies not named in the article and possibly some cocaine psychoses included, it is an average over very different cohorts. Lower figures come from a later Swedish register study (cumulative hazard 11.3% for all substance-induced psychoses) and from a 24-month trial (5.1%), consistent with broader case-finding, shorter follow-up or treated samples.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest in relation to the subject of the study (Acknowledgments).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from St George and Sutherland Hospitals (South Eastern Sydney Local Health District), the School of Psychiatry and the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre at the University of New South Wales, InforMH (System Information and Analytics Branch, NSW Ministry of Health) and the Northern Clinical School, University of Sydney. The review includes the corresponding author's register study (Sara et al., 2014), for which additional data were supplied, and a cohort co-authored by J. Lappin (Heslin et al., 2015); two authors also wrote a commentary arguing for assertive intervention in methamphetamine psychosis (Lappin, Sara and Farrell, 2017). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people with a first methamphetamine-induced psychosis, with a structured diagnosis at entry, family history and premorbid functioning recorded, urine-verified use and complete follow-up over several years, reporting the cumulative incidence of schizophrenia by continued use or abstinence and against a comparison group of people who use methamphetamine without psychosis.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people with substance-induced, brief, atypical, NOS or schizophreniform psychosis), comparisons (psychosis types; substances), outcome (later schizophrenia) and minimum follow-up are specified (Methods).
PROSPERO CRD42018086734; the protocol was not compared with the review here, and the article discusses no deviation except the planned meta-regressions that could not be done.
Case series, case-control and cohort studies and randomized trials were eligible without an explanation of the choice; all included studies were cohorts.

Three databases with the full search string, hand-searching of reference lists, and authors contacted for missing data; English-language peer-reviewed publications only, grey literature excluded, no registries, searches run by one author. The language limit is attributed to a lack of resources and expertise (Discussion › Limitations, 6th paragraph); the grey-literature exclusion is not justified. A strict reading would score 'no'; that would not change the overall rating recorded below.
Two authors selected the studies independently and resolved differences by consensus (Methods › Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria, 1st paragraph).
Two authors extracted all data independently, with a third resolving differences (Methods › Outcome and Moderator Variables, 2nd paragraph).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: 141 full texts were excluded (Results › Search Results, 1st paragraph); the article gives no list with reasons and the PRISMA chart is an image; whether the unopened supplement lists them is unknown.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, psychosis groups, transition proportion, sample size, age, sex, follow-up period and completeness, setting and diagnostic system and method for every study; the substance in each substance-induced cohort and the substance-specific estimates are not given in the article.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Newcastle–Ottawa Scale for cohort studies by two authors, with representativeness and diagnostic quality rated; per-study scores are not shown in the article, and how follow-up completeness and diagnostic relabelling were judged is not described.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects pooling within subgroups of logit-transformed proportions with z-based intervals, separate pools by psychosis type and by substance, and moderators analysed at study level because substance-specific estimates within a study are not independent (Methods › Meta-analysis). Judged met on balance, a close call: pooling cumulative proportions over follow-up of 1 to 20 years with I² of 96% to 99% is not justified in the text, and no prediction intervals are given.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: The effect of study quality was examined by median split, by each score value and by meta-regression (supplement), with no effect found (Results › Study Quality).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Diagnostic accuracy, heterogeneity, missing confounders and the language limit are discussed as limitations of the estimates (Discussion › Limitations), and the age association is flagged as possibly ecological; the conclusions are framed as risks of a later diagnosis.
Heterogeneity is quantified for every pool and explored by subgroup analysis and meta-regression; the limitations discuss why known risk factors were not detected.

Egger's test for each psychosis group (substance-induced intercept 3.02, P = .2966), funnel plots in the supplement, trim-and-fill not needed; the discussion reports no apparent impact (Results › Publication Bias; Table 5).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No external funding and no conflicts declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 can only be judged from the unopened supplement. If the supplement lists the 141 excluded full texts with reasons, the review has no critical flaw and three non-critical weaknesses (items 3, 8 and 10), which gives moderate confidence; if not, item 7 is a critical flaw and confidence is low, the rating recorded here until the supplement is read. Either way the pooled proportions are averages over extremely heterogeneous cohorts (I² 96% for amphetamines, 99% for all substance-induced psychoses) without prediction intervals. The review may be cited for the pooled transition figures by substance and for the absence of significant moderators; the amphetamine figure should be cited with its interval, its heterogeneity and the caveat that its component studies are not named in the article.

key_findings.finding: Registered (PROSPERO CRD42018086734) review following PRISMA and MOOSE: PsycINFO, MEDLINE and Embase searched via Ovid for English-language peer-reviewed publications from 1980 to 2018, with hand-searching of reference lists; two authors selected studies and extracted data independently; quality rated with the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale; authors of 16 studies were asked for subgroup data and 3 supplied them. The authors state that substance-induced is used by convention, not because a causal link is presumed.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Methods › Search Strategy; Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Outcome and Moderator Variables, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: 6097 records, 141 full texts excluded, 4 studies added by hand-searching: 50 cohort studies with 79 estimates in 40,783 people, 25 of them on substance-induced psychosis. Mean follow-up 4.0 years (range given as 1 to 20; 8.4 weighted by participants); mean 61% men (72% weighted); mean age 28 years; 25 countries; index diagnoses in hospital in 27 studies; all but 8 studies of first-episode cohorts.

Pooled proportion later diagnosed with schizophrenia: substance-induced psychosis 25% (95% CI 18% to 35%), 25 estimates, 34,224 people, I² 99%; brief, atypical and NOS psychoses 36% (30% to 43%); schizophreniform psychosis 65% (57% to 72%); all 79 estimates 44% (39% to 49%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pooled Rate of Transition to Schizophrenia, 1st paragraph; Table 2, upper panel

key_findings.finding: By substance (43 estimates from the 25 studies): amphetamines 22% (14% to 34%), 5 estimates, 2284 people, Q 106, I² 96%; cannabis 34% (25% to 46%), 6, 3040, I² 96%; hallucinogens 26% (14% to 43%), 3, 208; mixed or unspecified substances 22% (17% to 29%), 19, 8447; opioids 12% (8% to 18%), 3, 664; sedatives 10% (7% to 15%), 2, 223; alcohol 9% (6% to 15%), 5, 19,358. The substances differed (Q 137, df 6, P < .0001), and within-substance I² exceeded 90% wherever more than 3 samples were available.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pooled Rate of Transition to Schizophrenia, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, lower panel
key_findings.note: The five amphetamine estimates are not identified in the article, and the methods record methamphetamine, amphetamine and cocaine psychoses together as stimulant-induced (reporting issue 2).

key_findings.finding: No study characteristic predicted transition among the substance-induced psychoses at the Bonferroni threshold (P < .01): national 20% vs subnational 34% (P = .0559); urban 39% vs rural 19% vs mixed 22% (P = .0432); toxicology used 38% vs not 24% (P = .1423); study quality at or above the median 24% vs below 27% (P = .6683). In meta-regression, older cohorts had lower transition (β −0.050, −0.095 to −0.005, P = .0286), which the authors suggest may be ecological (more alcohol psychoses in older cohorts); sex, follow-up length (P = .3433), percentage followed up (β −1.716, −3.628 to 0.196, P = .0785) and publication year were not associated.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subgroup Analysis; Table 3; Table 4; Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Study quality did not change the estimates (median split, each score value and meta-regression), and Egger's test showed no small-study effect for substance-induced psychosis (intercept 3.02, t 1.07, P = .2966).
key_findings.locator: Results › Study Quality; Results › Publication Bias; Table 5

key_findings.finding: Table 1 entries relevant to methamphetamine: Kittirattanapaiboon (2010), Thailand, a cohort of methamphetamine psychosis after a first hospitalisation (reference 13): 39% with schizophrenia of 1116, follow-up 5.0 years with 40% followed up, hospital, file review. Medhus (listed as 2016; reference 72, a small prospective sample with amphetamine-induced psychosis, dated 2015): 33% of 29, 6.0 years, 41% followed up. Niemi-Pynttäri (2013), Finland, all substance-induced psychoses: 6% of 18,478, 6.2 years, 100%. Starzer, Denmark, all substance-induced psychoses: 17% of 6788, 20 years, 100%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (rows Kittirattanapaiboon, Medhus, Niemi-Pynttari, Starzer); References 13, 16, 17 and 72
key_findings.note: Substance-specific figures for these studies (for example the amphetamine subgroup of the Finnish register) are not given in the article.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: very few studies reported the amount or duration of substance use before the episode, comorbid substance use disorders or continued use during follow-up, although ongoing use is likely a critical risk factor; most diagnoses came from registers or routine care (file review 7 studies and 19,038 people; clinical diagnosis 10 and 15,059), with research interviews in only 8 studies and 127 people; English-language publications only.

Three studies gave within-study estimates for cannabis and other substances; all found the highest transition after cannabis-induced psychosis, although in one the difference from stimulants was not significant. A later Swedish national study (Kendler et al., 2019) reported cumulative hazards of 11.3% for all substance-induced psychoses and 18.0% for cannabis, and familial risk scores twice as high in those who transitioned.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Cannabis and Transition to Schizophrenia, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The number of people with substance-induced psychosis is 34,224 in Table 2, where the seven substance subgroups also sum to 34,224 (editors' sum), but 34,244 in the abstract, the Results and the Discussion.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Results › Search Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 2; Discussion, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Table 2's figure should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods record methamphetamine, amphetamine and cocaine psychoses together as stimulant-induced, but the results and abstract report an amphetamines subgroup, and no stimulant or cocaine category appears; the five amphetamine estimates and the studies behind them are not named in the article.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria, 2nd paragraph; Abstract; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the 22% (14% to 34%) includes cocaine-induced psychoses, and which methamphetamine cohorts it contains, cannot be determined without the supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: Follow-up is said to range from 1 to 20 years, but Table 1 lists 0.5 years for Baldwin (2005) and 0.0 years for Rahm (2007), whose title in the reference list describes diagnostic stability over 3 years; the Rahm row also gives a mean age of 0 and 0% men.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Search Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 (Baldwin and Rahm rows); reference 41
reporting_issues.consequence: Missing values appear to be printed as zeros; the table's follow-up and demographic columns cannot be summed or averaged without checking each entry.

reporting_issues.issue: Some Table 1 years differ from the reference list (Medhus 2016 vs 2015 in reference 72; Starzer 2017 vs 2018 in reference 17), and the Medhus cohort is given as 29 people where the 2019 systematic review gives 28 for the same study (study card sc_voce_2019).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the same small cohort enters different reviews with different numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's sample sizes are whole-cohort sizes rather than the subgroups analysed: Sara (2014) is listed with 43,968 people, more than the 40,783 in the whole analysis, and Niemi-Pynttäri (2013) with 18,478 for all substances.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 (Sara and Niemi-Pynttari rows); Results › Search Results, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of people each study contributes to each pooled estimate cannot be read from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports that transition rates were slightly lower in older cohorts, a meta-regression with P = .0286, while the review set P < .01 as the threshold for its planned subgroup comparisons; no threshold is stated for the meta-regressions. In Table 3 the between-group I² column shows 99 for every moderator.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Methods › Meta-analysis, 2nd paragraph; Table 3; Table 4
reporting_issues.consequence: The age association is weaker evidence than the abstract implies (the discussion calls it possibly ecological); the repeated 99 appears to be the overall I² rather than a between-group statistic.
